title: Pure water into pure water
theme: As pure water poured into pure water becomes just the same, so becomes the self of the sage who knows, Gautama.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «एकरसमेव नान्यथा», of one taste, not otherwise; Raṅgarāmānuja: «तत्सदृशमेव», just like it; Madhva: like it, «न तु स एव», not the same

words.role: main verb; tādṛk eva is understood

sandhi.rule: A final k becomes g before a vowel, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

sandhi.type: visarga after e before a voiced sound; aḥ before a vowel
sandhi.rule: The visarga from s after a vowel other than a becomes r before a voiced sound (P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः)); the visarga of -aḥ is lost before a vowel other than a, and the vowels stay apart.

morphology.note: From tad + dṛś, ‘looking like that’: ‘such, of that kind’. The pausal form of tādṛś is tādṛk; before eva it becomes tādṛg. It is the word on which the readings divide: ‘just that’ or ‘just like that’.
The present participle of vi-√jñā, ‘know, discern’, genitive singular, agreeing with muneḥ.
Vocative of Gautama, ‘descendant of Gotama’: Death addresses Naciketas by his family name, as at 2.2.6.

translation.literal: As pure water poured into pure water becomes just such, so becomes the self of the sage who knows, O Gautama.
translation.readable: As clear water poured into clear water becomes just the same, so, Gautama, becomes the self of the sage who knows.

anvaya: यथा शुद्धे [उदके] आसिक्तम् शुद्धम् उदकम् तादृक् एव भवति, एवम् [हे] गौतम, विजानतः मुनेः आत्मा [तादृक् एव] भवति ।
syntax: A comparison: yathā … bhavati (the image) and evam … bhavati (the application). tādṛg eva, the predicate of the first clause, is understood in the second. gautama is a vocative.

ambiguities.topic: ‘Becomes just such’: the same, or like?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: of one taste, not otherwise — the self of the knower is one with the self, «एकरसमेव नान्यथा, तादृगेव भवति»; Raṅgarāmānuja: the purified self becomes equal to the pure supreme Self, «विशुद्धेन परमात्मना समानो भवतीत्यर्थः»; Madhva: it becomes like him, not the same, «न तु स एव भवति». This is the verse on which the three schools' doctrines of release most plainly part.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Counted as written, 18 and 16 syllables. The first half-line has two syllables over the norm: yathodakaṃ śuddhe śuddham (8) āsiktaṃ tādṛg eva bhavati (10). The second half-line is regular.

beginner: The vallī ends with a simple, beautiful image. Pour clear water into clear water, and it does not stay apart: it becomes just like the water it joins. So, Death tells Naciketas, becomes the self of the sage who truly knows. The great commentators read this one image in three ways, and here their teachings on liberation show most clearly. Śaṅkara says the knower's self becomes one with the supreme Self, with nothing left to divide them; he calls the Veda kinder than a thousand mothers and fathers for teaching it. Raṅgarāmānuja says the purified self becomes equal to the pure supreme Self, alike in purity. Madhva says it becomes like the Lord, never the same as him; even the highest of souls reaches only likeness.
analogy: Like a cup of clear water poured into a clear pool: one can no longer point to where the cupful is.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: As pure water poured into pure water becomes just such, so becomes the self of the sage who knows.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: For the knower whose seeing of difference made by adjuncts is destroyed, who sees the self as «विशुद्धविज्ञानघनैकरसमद्वयमात्मानं», pure water poured into pure water is of one taste, not otherwise, «एकरसमेव नान्यथा»; so the self of the sage who knows oneness becomes. Therefore one should give up the divisive views of bad reasoners and of those who deny the Veda, and honour the seeing of the self's oneness taught by the Veda, which wishes us more good than a thousand mothers and fathers: «मातृपितृसहस्रेभ्योऽपि हितैषिणा वेदेनोपदिष्टमात्मैकत्वदर्शनं».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: equal to the pure Self
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The verse states the fruit of knowing that all has one self, «सर्वत्रैकात्मकत्वज्ञानस्य फलमाह». Pure water joined to pure water becomes like it, «तत्सदृशमेव भवति, न कथञ्चिदपि विसदृशम्»; so the self of one who knows, purified by the knowledge of the supreme Self, becomes equal to the pure supreme Self, «विशुद्धेन परमात्मना समानो भवतीत्यर्थः». Death calls ‘Gautama’ with joy, hinting at the greatness of what is to be reached.

commentary.q: Madhva: like him, not the same
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The self of the knowing sage — even Vāyu — becomes such, not the same: «विजानतो मुनेरात्मा वायुरपि तादृगेव भवति न तु स एव भवति»; how much less other souls, «किम्वन्ये जीवाः». He cites verses he attributes to the Bhaviṣyat-parvan: the released Vāyu reaches likeness to Viṣṇu, «मुक्तो वायुश्च सादृश्यमेवं विष्णोस्तु गच्छति», and not his form, «न तु तद्रूपतां याति».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: tādṛk, ‘looking like that’, can mean ‘just such’ in kind or ‘just like’ in resemblance; the Sanskrit does not decide between identity and likeness, and each school takes it in the sense its doctrine of release requires.

advaita.text: The knower's self becomes of one taste with the self, «एकरसमेव नान्यथा»: release is the realised oneness of the self, and the Veda's teaching of it is to be honoured, «आत्मैकत्वदर्शनं शान्तदर्पैरादरणीयमित्यर्थः».

visistadvaita.text: The released self becomes equal to the supreme Self in purity, «विशुद्धेन परमात्मना समानो भवतीत्यर्थः» — like it, never unlike it, and still a self.

dvaita.text: The released self, even the highest, Vāyu, attains likeness to Viṣṇu, not identity, «न तु स एव भवति».

schools.disagreement: Identity (Śaṅkara: of one taste, not otherwise), equality in purity (Raṅgarāmānuja: samāna), likeness and not identity (Madhva: tādṛg eva, na tu sa eva). The image of water in water serves all three; the word tādṛk does not settle the question.

parallels.quote: यथा नद्यः स्यन्दमानाः समुद्रेऽस्तं गच्छन्ति नामरूपे विहाय
parallels.note: The Muṇḍaka's image of release: rivers losing name and form in the ocean.

contemporary.text: People describe deep understanding as merging, belonging, or coming home, and also as meeting something other than oneself. The single image of water poured into water holds both, which may be why three schools could each find their teaching in it. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: Have you ever felt so at home somewhere that you could not tell where you ended and it began?
reflect.deeper: Śaṅkara, Raṅgarāmānuja and Madhva all accept the image of water poured into water. What does each keep, and what does each refuse, in it?
reflect.practice: Pour a little water into a glass of water and watch it closely; then sit for a minute with what you saw.

references.text: In madhva.json the entry for 2.1.15 begins with the colophon of Madhva's bhāṣya on this vallī (॥ इति काठकोपनिषद्भाष्ये द्वितीयाध्याये प्रथमावल्ली समाप्ता ॥), which precedes his comment on 2.1.15 in the source; the colophon is not quoted as his comment. Raṅgarāmānuja's entry likewise opens with his vallī colophon.

flags.note: Identity (Śaṅkara), equality in purity (Raṅgarāmānuja), likeness (Madhva) — the three doctrines of release, set side by side; the verse's tādṛk does not decide between them.
